questions.q: What are the four settings in which design and production take place, in order of increasing scale and formality (the hook DCIC)?
options: Domestic, Commercial, Industrial, Community
Domestic, Community, Industrial, Commercial
Design, Construction, Industry, Commerce
Domestic, Cooperative, Institutional, Corporate
questions.explanation: The four settings are Domestic, Community, Industrial and Commercial — remember DCIC, a ladder climbing from the smallest and most informal (someone making something at home) up to the largest and most formal (a company mass-producing for a market).

questions.q: Which description best defines a domestic setting?
options: A community group or cooperative producing for the common good rather than profit
Design and production based in a home or small workshop, usually small-scale or one-off, using simple tools to keep costs low
Large-scale production using a divided workforce and large-scale machinery
Design and production driven by a market and the goal of selling competitively for profit
questions.explanation: A domestic setting is home- or small-workshop-based, small-scale or one-off, with simple tools and low cost — the kitchen-table start-up, like cake designer Faye Cahill beginning from home. The other options describe the community, industrial and commercial settings respectively.

questions.q: What single feature distinguishes a community setting from the other three settings?
options: It always produces goods on the largest possible scale
It is not primarily intent on making a profit — it aims to provide a service or benefit for the common good of local people
It uses the most sophisticated, automated machinery available
It relies entirely on overseas markets and exports
questions.explanation: The defining feature the exam loves is the motive: a community setting (a co-op or interest group) works for the common good — local jobs, fresh produce — rather than primarily for profit. A community garden is the textbook example. Describing it by scale instead of motive is the trap.

questions.q: Why does a designer need to consider the industrial and commercial practices that will be used during manufacturing?
options: To ensure the product will sell
To gain access to cheaper resources
To increase the product's rate of production
To produce products that meet market needs
questions.explanation: Understanding industrial and commercial manufacturing practices lets a designer plan for efficient mass production and a higher rate of production. The other options are commercial outcomes that depend on, but are not the direct reason for, considering these practices.

questions.q: Across all four settings, what stays the same and what changes?
options: The design process changes; the scale of production stays the same
The design process (DRIPER) stays the same; the scale, resources, division of labour and formality change
Both the process and the scale stay the same in every setting
Each setting uses a fundamentally different process invented for that scale
questions.explanation: The backbone of the topic: every setting runs the same design process — define, research, ideate, produce, evaluate, refine. What differs is the scale of production, company size, resources and machinery, division of labour, formality and the amount of documentation and quality control. A factory does not use a different process from a home maker — just far more resources and rigour.

questions.q: Although industrial and commercial settings overlap, what distinction should an answer signal between them?
options: Industrial is for profit, while commercial is for the common good
Industrial emphasises the large-scale making of goods, while commercial emphasises the business of selling them in a market
Industrial works at small scale, while commercial works at large scale
Industrial uses simple tools, while commercial uses no machinery at all
questions.explanation: Industrial leans on the making — large-scale, mechanised manufacture — while commercial leans on the selling: design driven by a market, a target customer and profit, so market research and marketing loom large. A company often does both, but blurring the two (or forgetting the community setting) is the classic trap.

questions.q: From memory: across the four settings, what stays the same and what changes? Name both before you reveal.
keyPoints: What stays the same: the design process itself (DRIPER) — every setting must define a need, research, ideate, produce, evaluate and refine.
What changes: the scale of production, the size of the operation, the resources and machinery available, the division of labour, the formality, and the amount of documentation and quality control.
The core mark is simply: 'the process is the same but the scale changes.'
questions.explanation: If you recalled that DRIPER is constant and listed several variables (scale, resources, labour, formality, QC), grade yourself Good or Easy. If you only said 'a factory is bigger', that vague single point caps low — grade Again or Hard.

questions.q: From memory: name the four settings (DCIC) and a one-word tag for each.
keyPoints: Domestic — the home (small-scale or one-off, simple tools).
Community — the co-op (for the common good, not primarily for profit).
Commercial — the market (design and production driven by selling for profit).
questions.explanation: Pairing each setting with a one-word tag protects you if a follow-up asks you to describe one. If you got all four names and tags, grade Good or Easy.

questions.q: Explain why the design process remains the same across different settings while the scale of production differs. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: The design process remains the same because every setting must still define a need, research, generate and develop ideas, produce a solution, and evaluate and refine it — this sequence is fundamental to creating any successful design regardless of where it happens. What differs is the scale and the resources: the size of the operation, the workforce, the machinery and the funds available, which determine how many units are produced and how formally. So the same process is simply executed with more people, equipment, documentation and rigour as the setting grows from domestic to industrial.

criteria.descriptor: States that the design process (define, research, ideate, produce, evaluate, refine) is fundamental and universal to every setting.
Identifies that scale and resources — operation size, workforce, machinery, funds — are what differ between settings.
Explains that the setting changes the execution (more people, equipment, documentation, rigour), not the process itself.

questions.explanation: This is the central insight of the topic: same process, different variables. The mark rewards stating the process is constant, naming what differs, and linking the difference to execution rather than the process.

questions.q:
Mass production is the process of creating goods on a large scale and with limited human input.

Explain how the trend towards mass production may affect workplace practices.
questions.modelAnswer: Mass production reshapes workplace practices in both positive and negative ways. Processes such as robotics, CNC machinery and automation increase the speed and accuracy of producing goods, from injection-moulded plastics to small-batch items, and allow extended hours of operation and total quality management. However, the same trend forces job transition and the upskilling of employees, and can lead to job losses and higher unemployment, affecting individuals' wellbeing and society at large as the nature of work changes with technological advancement.

criteria.descriptor: Provides a comprehensive explanation of the effects of the mass production trend on workplace practices
Provides an explanation of the effects the mass production trend has on workplace practices
Provides a description of the effects the mass production trend has on workplace practices
Demonstrates some understanding of the effects the mass production trend has on workplace practices

questions.explanation: Mass production is the hallmark of the industrial setting — large-scale, mechanised making with a divided workforce. A strong answer balances the gains (speed, accuracy, automation, extended operation, quality management) against the costs (job transition, upskilling, job losses, changed nature of work).
